title: Weak Spine Linked with Greater Cognitive Decline
paragraphs: As people get older, both their bones and their brains tend to weaken. Now, a new study from the United States suggests that these two changes may be connected. According to the research, people with weaker bones in their spine may experience faster cognitive decline.

The study was carried out by a team at Johns Hopkins University, including the radiologists Shadpour Demehri and Sara Momtazmanesh, and it was published in the journal Radiology in 2026. The researchers analyzed existing data on 715 people from a long-running health research project.

First, the researchers measured the participants' bone mineral density, which shows how strong bones are, in the spine. To do this, they used chest CT scans and a specially developed artificial intelligence program. The participants also took tests of their thinking and memory. Several years later, they had brain scans and took the cognitive tests again.

The researchers found that people with lower bone density in their spine showed more signs of damage in certain areas of the brain's white matter. These areas have previously been linked to important skills such as attention, working memory and planning. In addition, people with lower bone density tended to show a faster decline in their scores on the thinking tests.

However, the researchers stressed that the study does not show that weak bones cause cognitive decline. As Demehri put it, the study is not about cause and effect. Instead, the researchers believe that both problems may be caused by the same underlying factors, such as problems with the body's metabolism. Possible examples include insulin resistance, unhealthy levels of fats in the blood and the changes that happen during menopause.
According to Momtazmanesh, chest scans that are already taken for other reasons could be used to measure bone density in the spine and identify people who may be at risk of cognitive decline.

Nevertheless, much more research is needed before this could be used as a screening tool. Scientists also do not yet know whether the faster brain aging seen in the study leads to conditions such as dementia.
